bibliography.abstract: Truck–vulnerable road user (VRU) collisions are among the most severe and fatal crashes, yet novice truck drivers receive limited training on hazard anticipation in VRU-related scenarios. This study presents and evaluates the effectiveness of a newly developed video-based VRU-hazard anticipation training module for novice truck drivers. Using a truck driving simulator and eye tracker, we assessed participants’ performance in eight hazardous scenarios before and after training, and compared results with a control group who received placebo training. Measures included glance behaviour towards areas of interest (AOIs) relevant to VRU safety (time to first glance, percent of time looking, average and maximum glance durations), as well as driving metrics (average speed and maximum deceleration). Results indicate that hazard-trained drivers spent a significantly larger proportion of time attending to VRU-relevant AOIs compared to their pre-training performance and placebo-trained participants. Driving behaviour measures showed no statistically significant changes, but hazard-trained drivers had lower speeds and smoother decelerations, descriptively. Additionally, participants’ self-evaluation of how safe of a driver they are was negatively associated with glance metrics, suggesting that drivers who may have overconfidence in their abilities may require further attention. Overall, the findings demonstrate that hazard anticipation training can enhance novice truck drivers’ attention allocation towards VRUs, supporting its potential of enhancing entry-level training. Future research should explore larger samples, long-term retention, the effect of VRU-hazard anticipation training on experienced drivers, and more varied hazard scenarios.
bibliography.title: Developing and testing the effectiveness of a truck driver hazard anticipation training module: a simulator study

en.caveats: The study relied on a simulator environment rather than real-world driving conditions, and the abstract does not disclose the sample size used to establish statistical significance.
en.what: The study developed and evaluated a video-based hazard anticipation training module for novice truck drivers using a truck driving simulator and eye-tracking technology. Researchers measured driving metrics and glance behaviors across eight hazardous scenarios involving vulnerable road users (VRUs) before and after training, comparing a treatment group to a placebo control group. The trained drivers spent a significantly higher percentage of time looking at VRU-relevant areas of interest, though changes in driving speed and deceleration metrics were not statistically significant.
en.why: It demonstrates that a targeted, video-based training intervention can measurably improve how novice truck drivers allocate their attention toward vulnerable road users, offering a concrete method to enhance entry-level commercial driver safety programs.
